design_detail: Case-comparator laboratory study. Bronchoalveolar-lavage (BAL) fluid from 51 patients with e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) in 16 US states, collected August to December 2019 during routine clinical care and sent to CDC through state health departments, compared with BAL fluid from 99 healthy participants of an unrelated Ohio State University study (52 who neither vaped nor smoked, 18 who vaped nicotine only, 29 who smoked cigarettes only; sampled 2016 to 2019, 90 before 2019). CDC measured by isotope-dilution mass spectrometry a list of priority substances chosen in advance: vitamin E acetate, plant oils (long-chain triglycerides), medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil, coconut oil, petroleum distillates and diluent terpenes including limonene; also THC, nicotine and their metabolites, and a lung-surfactant marker (DPPC) to confirm that each sample held lung lining fluid. Results are counts and percentages; no statistical tests or intervals are given. Version read: the author manuscript of the New England Journal of Medicine article.
can_establish: In a convenience sample of 51 patients with EVALI and 99 healthy volunteers, how often vitamin E acetate and a list of other suspected additives were found in lung lavage fluid: vitamin E acetate in 48 of 51 patients and in none of the volunteers, and each other additive in at most one patient.
cannot_establish: Whether vitamin E acetate caused the injury (no dose, timing or experiment; the comparison group contained no one who vaped THC products and was not ill, so the finding could reflect the 2019 supply of THC cartridges rather than the injury); anything about substances not on the chosen list (the analysis was targeted); what product a patient used or where it came from (lavage does not show it); how typical the 51 are of the more than 2,400 patients hospitalized (lavage was done by clinicians' choice, without a standard protocol); and how long after the last use the fluid was taken.

sample.recruitment: Patients: BAL fluid obtained by hospital clinical teams for patient care on a case-by-case basis, sent to CDC by state health departments in 16 states (Arizona 2, Arkansas 2, California 4, Connecticut 1, Hawaii 1, Illinois 12, Indiana 1, Maryland 4, Michigan 2, Minnesota 5, Missouri 1, North Carolina 2, Texas 2, Utah 3, West Virginia 1, Wisconsin 8); accepted if the health department classified the person as a confirmed or probable case; no other criteria. Comparators: recruited through local media and participant registries for a tobacco-product study at Ohio State University, aged 21 to 45, with no major clinical illness or increased risk from bronchoscopy (Methods › Biospecimen collection).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cases met the CDC EVALI case definitions as judged by state or local health officials: use of an e-cigarette or dabbing in the 90 days before symptom onset, a lung infiltrate or ground-glass opacity on imaging, and exclusion of infection and other plausible diagnoses (confirmed), or infection present but judged not the sole cause or testing incomplete (probable) (Table 1).
sample.demographics: Patients: median age 23 (range 16 to 67), 35 of 51 (69%) male. Of 43 with information on product use, 7 (16%) reported nicotine products only, 11 (26%) THC products only and 22 (51%) both (the three others are not accounted for). Comparators: median age 26 (range 21 to 44); 53 of 99 (54%) male; none reported vaping THC products (Table 2).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Lung-fluid volumes were small in some samples, so analytes were prioritized (vitamin E acetate first) and results for the others are not available for all; denominators run from 12 (petroleum distillates) to 51 (Table 3). Product-use information was available for 43 of 51 patients.
sample.selection_effects: The 51 are about 2% of the more than 2,400 patients hospitalized by 12 December 2019 and were sampled when a clinical team judged BAL useful; they are called a convenience sample by the authors. The comparators are healthy volunteers from one Ohio study with different eligibility, sampled mostly before 2019, and include nobody who vaped THC (Methods; Results, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Laboratory: isotope-dilution mass spectrometry in BAL fluid, with limits of detection estimated from repeated measures at zero concentration; results above the limit are positive. Methods were validated by CDC for accuracy, precision, sensitivity and specificity (details in Supplementary Table S1, a PDF that was not opened). Self-reported vaping in the 90 days before illness comes from interviews, available for 43 of 51 patients.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured: concentrations in the fluid are not reported, only presence or absence; time from last vaping to bronchoscopy was unavailable; no product testing in this study.
exposure.polysubstance: Patients commonly used multiple tobacco and cannabis products. THC or its metabolites were found in BAL fluid from 40 of 47 patients (85%) and nicotine or its metabolites in 30 of 47 (64%). Of 11 patients who reported no THC product use in the 90 days before illness, 9 had THC or its metabolites in BAL fluid. 47 of 50 (94%) had THC in BAL fluid or reported vaping THC products.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable for patients (time since last vaping unknown). Comparators' non-smoking status was confirmed by urine anatabine.

comparison.controls: 99 healthy volunteers from an unrelated study at Ohio State University (52 who neither vaped nor smoked; 18 who vaped nicotine only; 29 who smoked cigarettes only), sampled 2016 to 2019 with 90 of the 99 samples taken before 2019, processed by that study's laboratory within 30 minutes of collection.
comparison.matching: None. Patients: median age 23, 69% male, from 16 states; comparators: median age 26, 54% male, from one Ohio study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Time between last vaping and the lavage; treatment before the lavage; underlying lung disease; what products patients used, from where, and in what amount; no comparison group of people who vaped THC (including cartridges) without injury.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Urine THC biomarkers were positive in 21 of 82 tested comparators (26%), and BAL THC biomarkers in 5.1% of comparators (5 of 99); nicotine or metabolites were found in 52% of comparators' BAL fluid. No comparator reported vaping THC.

outcomes.instruments: Isotope-dilution mass spectrometry for each priority substance in Table 3: vitamin E acetate, MCT oil, coconut oil, plant oil, squalane, squalene, alpha-pinene, beta-pinene, 3-carene, limonene, petroleum distillates; also THC, nicotine and metabolites and the surfactant lipid DPPC, which was detectable in every sample and used as the adequacy marker. EVALI case status was assigned by state or local health officials.
outcomes.validity_norms: Methods met or exceeded US clinical laboratory quality criteria, according to the authors. The authors note that vitamin E acetate and other oils may be missed if BAL fluid was not well mixed, which they could not check, and that samples were collected under each hospital's own routine and not standardized.
outcomes.operationalization: Positive means above the limit of detection; no quantities are reported. Case status is the health department's classification under a definition the authors call intentionally sensitive; EVALI is a diagnosis of exclusion with no confirmatory test.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; no statistical tests are reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Vitamin E acetate in BAL fluid: 48 of 51 patients (94%), 0 of 52 comparators who neither vaped nor smoked, 0 of 18 who vaped nicotine, 0 of 29 who smoked cigarettes, 0 of 99 in all. Editors' calculation, exact binomial 95% intervals: patients 83.8% to 98.8%; comparators 0% to 3.7%. All three patients without vitamin E acetate were probable cases, so all 25 confirmed cases were positive (editors' deduction; 25 of 25, interval 86.3% to 100%) and 23 of 26 probable cases. Other priority substances in patients: coconut oil 1 of 48, limonene 1 of 39, MCT oil 0 of 49, plant oil 0 of 49, squalane 0 of 38, squalene 0 of 38, alpha-pinene 0 of 39, beta-pinene 0 of 39, 3-carene 0 of 39, petroleum distillates 0 of 12; none in comparators (denominators 17 to 98 per substance). THC or metabolites in BAL fluid of patients: 40 of 47 (85%); nicotine or metabolites 30 of 47 (64%).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a public health response activity: CDC determined this information collection did not meet the regulatory definition of research. The comparators' study is registered (NCT02596685, cited in the reference list; not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: All priority substances on the pre-set list are shown in Table 3, the three vitamin E acetate-negative patients are described in Table 4, and the limitations are stated. Results for substances other than vitamin E acetate were not available for every sample because of small volumes.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Vitamin E acetate was found in the lung lavage fluid of 48 of 51 patients with EVALI from 16 states and in none of 99 healthy volunteers, none of whom vaped THC products; nearly none of the other pre-listed additives were found in patients; the three patients without it were all probable cases with other plausible diagnoses recorded; THC or its metabolites were found in 85% of patients, including 9 of 11 who said they had not used THC products.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that vitamin E acetate was associated with EVALI in a convenience sample of 51 patients; the Discussion says it may play a role and lists four supports (high detection in 16 states, absence in healthy comparators, absence of other priority substances, a plausible mechanism and timing with the illicit market). It states that the absence of the other listed substances is evidence against their being a primary cause. Gaps: (1) the healthy comparators included no one who vaped THC, so the contrast cannot separate vitamin E acetate from vaping of THC products in 2019 in general; (2) the absence of other substances is for a targeted list, with 12 to 49 samples for some; (3) the mechanism (loss of surfactant function; heated vitamin E acetate forming ketene) and the supply timing (Minnesota seizures, trade websites, FDA product testing) are from other sources, not tested here; (4) the authors themselves say vitamin E acetate may be a marker for another toxicant and that animal studies are needed to show cause. The paper's wording is cautious ('associated', 'may play a role').

timeline.event: New York State Department of Health (press release, 5 September 2019) reported vitamin E acetate in THC-containing products used by 34 persons with lung illness; the FDA and Minnesota seizure testing are cited as finding it in product fluids (49% of case-associated THC product samples; 20 of 20 THC products seized in September 2019 against 0 of 10 in 2018). Second-hand here: cited, not read.

CDC's earlier report of 29 patients in 10 states, all with vitamin E acetate in BAL fluid (MMWR, cited in this paper's references); this study extends that work and presumably includes those patients, so the two are not independent.
Analysis of illicit THC vaping cartridges recovered from patients in New York State

replication.where_it_stands: The lung-fluid finding comes from one laboratory (CDC) and overlapping patients; the product-level findings come from several laboratories but are cited second-hand in this paper. Whether vitamin E acetate alone causes the injury is stated by the authors to need animal studies.

funding.funder: National Cancer Institute grant P50CA180908; FDA Center for Tobacco Products grant P30CA016058; Ohio State University Pelotonia Intramural Research (Acknowledgments). The paper states that the content is solely the authors' responsibility and does not necessarily represent the views of the National Institutes of Health, CDC or FDA.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the text read: the authors' disclosure forms are on the publisher's site and were not opened.
funding.affiliations_note: Most authors work in CDC laboratory and response units, the agency that led the outbreak investigation and gave the public advice discussed; one author is affiliated with the FDA and several with Ohio State University. A government health agency, not the cannabis or tobacco industry.

what_would_settle_it: A study that tests lung fluid or breath from people who vape THC cartridges with and without injury, matched for time and source, with product contents measured, quantities reported and a wide untargeted chemical screen; plus controlled animal and human-tissue exposure to the aerosol of vitamin E acetate with and without THC, at realistic temperatures.

domains.note: Patients (hospitalized across 16 states in 2019) and comparators (healthy volunteers in Ohio, mostly sampled before 2019) differ in age, sex, setting, collection protocol and time, and none of the comparators vaped THC; nothing is adjusted. The contrast cannot separate vitamin E acetate from THC cartridge use in 2019 or from the illness itself.

Validated mass spectrometry with limits of detection and an adequacy marker in every sample, but patients' samples were collected without a standard protocol, at an unknown interval after last use and after treatment, and the authors could not check that fluid was mixed well; only the vitamin E acetate result is available for all, and others have denominators of 12 to 49.

51 patients, about 2% of those hospitalized, whose clinicians chose to do a lavage; comparators from an unrelated study with its own eligibility, 21 to 45 years, no major illness; nobody who vaped THC and was well.

Treatments given before the lavage (for example antibiotics or glucocorticoids, which Table 4 lists for three patients) and their timing are not reported; the interval from last use to lavage is unknown.

Small volumes limited the analytes measured per sample (12 to 49 patients for substances other than vitamin E acetate); product-use history is missing for 8 of 51; time since last use is not available.

Case status was assigned by health departments under a definition the authors call intentionally sensitive, for a diagnosis of exclusion; 26 of 51 are probable cases and the three without vitamin E acetate are all probable cases with other plausible diagnoses in Table 4.
A descriptive report in which every pre-listed substance and the three negative patients are shown; no protocol, but no sign of selective reporting.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain; confounding and selection are high because the two groups come from different populations and times and the comparators do not include people who vaped THC without injury. The laboratory method is validated, the target substance was measured in every sample, the counts are plain and the limitations are stated by the authors. It may be cited for the finding that vitamin E acetate was present in the lung fluid of 48 of 51 patients from 16 states and in none of 99 healthy volunteers, that all 25 confirmed cases were positive, and that the other listed additives were almost never found. It may not be cited as proof of cause, for lung fluid in people who vape THC products without injury, for substances not on the list, for the national proportion, or for any product or source.

key_findings.finding: BAL fluid was obtained from 51 patients with EVALI in 16 states (August to December 2019) and from 99 healthy participants of an unrelated Ohio State University study (52 neither vaping nor smoking, 18 vaping nicotine only, 29 smoking cigarettes only; sampled 2016 to 2019, 90 before 2019). Case status was confirmed for 25 and probable for 26 patients; median age 23 (range 16 to 67), 69% male; BAL fluid came from 3 patients who later died.
key_findings.note: Author manuscript version of the NEJM article.

key_findings.finding: Vitamin E acetate was found in BAL fluid from 48 of 51 patients (94%) and from none of the 99 healthy participants (0 of 52, 0 of 18, 0 of 29). Editors' calculation, exact 95% interval for patients 83.8% to 98.8%, for comparators 0% to 3.7%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3 (vitamin E acetate row)

key_findings.finding: Other priority substances in patients' BAL fluid: coconut oil 1 of 48 and limonene 1 of 39 (the limonene patient had no vitamin E acetate or THC and reported daily flavoured nicotine products); MCT oil, plant oil, squalane, squalene, pinenes, 3-carene 0 of 38 to 49; petroleum distillates 0 of 12. None of these was found in any comparator.

The three patients without detectable vitamin E acetate were all probable cases. Table 4 lists for them unintentional multidrug overdose with benzodiazepines and oxycodone and suspected vaping lung injury (patient 1), acute eosinophilic pneumonia later revised to coccidioidomycosis with or without EVALI (patient 2), and acute hypoxic respiratory failure with Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia attributed to vaping lung injury (patient 3). The two interviewed denied vaping THC products. All 25 confirmed cases were therefore positive (editors' deduction).

THC or its metabolites were found in BAL fluid of 40 of 47 patients (85%); 9 of 11 patients who reported no THC product use in the 90 days before illness had THC or metabolites in BAL fluid; 47 of 50 (94%) had THC in BAL fluid or reported vaping THC products. Nicotine or metabolites were found in 30 of 47 (64%). Self-reported (43 patients): nicotine products only 7 (16%), THC products only 11 (26%), both 22 (51%).

Among healthy comparators, urine THC biomarkers were positive in 25.6% (21 of 82) and BAL THC biomarkers in 5.1%; nicotine or metabolites in 52% of BAL fluids. No comparator reported vaping THC. All comparators' BAL fluid was negative for every priority substance.

Context quoted from other sources (second-hand): as of 12 December 2019, more than 2,400 hospitalized patients across all 50 states, Washington DC and two territories and 52 deaths in 25 states and Washington DC (CDC web page); 78% under 35; symptoms over days to weeks, respiratory 95%, constitutional 85%, gastrointestinal 77%; nearly half (47%) needed intensive care for respiratory failure (Siegel et al., not read). New York State laboratory testing of THC-containing products used by 34 persons with lung illness found vitamin E acetate in at least one product for each; FDA testing found it in 49% of case-associated THC product samples, on average 50% by weight (range 23% to 88%), and in none of 197 case-associated nicotine products; in Minnesota, 0 of 10 products seized in 2018 contained it against 20 of 20 THC products seized in September 2019.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: These figures are the authors' citations of a CDC web page, a New York State press release, FDA web pages and an MMWR report; none was read for this card.

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: vitamin E acetate may be a marker of another toxicant (which would have to correlate with it, be widespread in the US and have entered THC product fluids in 2019); aerosol products from heating vitamin E acetate (for example ketene) are not examined; sample collection was not standardized; timing and burden of exposure relative to the sample could not be assessed; case and comparator samples come from independent studies at single time points, so unknown confounding remains. Animal studies are needed to show whether vitamin E acetate alone causes the injury.

Reports cited by the authors say that diluents such as vitamin E acetate and MCT oil are added to THC-containing products to improve appearance, aroma or taste and lower cost, and that adding vitamin E acetate to product fluid appeared in the illicit market in late 2018 or early 2019 and became more common in 2019 (trade websites and laboratory reports; second-hand).
key_findings.note: Trade-website and press sources, not peer-reviewed.

key_findings.finding: Funding: NCI P50CA180908, FDA Center for Tobacco Products P30CA016058, Ohio State University Pelotonia Intramural Research. Authors' disclosure forms are on the publisher's site (not read).

Case definitions as printed in the paper (Table 1): confirmed and probable cases both need vaping or dabbing in the 90 days before symptom onset, a lung infiltrate on chest X-ray or CT, and no evidence in the medical record of an alternative plausible diagnosis (for example cardiac, rheumatologic or neoplastic). Confirmed cases also need negative respiratory viral and influenza tests and negative results on all other clinically indicated infectious-disease tests; probable cases may have an infection identified, or incomplete testing, if the clinical team judges that the infection is not the sole cause of the lung injury. State and local health departments assigned case status.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Case Definitions; Table 1 (Case Definitions for Patients with EVALI)
key_findings.note: Added after the claim draft needed the definition; the CDC update (Krishnasamy 2020) cites the definition by reference only.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives self-reported product use for 43 patients as nicotine only 7, THC only 11 and both 22, which sum to 40; the other 3 (7%) are not accounted for.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably patients who reported neither type of product (for example other substances); the paper does not say. The text's 77% THC and 67% nicotine are taken from the same three cells (33 of 43 and 29 of 43).

reporting_issues.issue: Substance results other than vitamin E acetate have varying denominators (petroleum distillates 12 of 51; coconut oil 48; squalane 38; pinenes 39), because small volumes meant analytes were prioritized.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3; Methods › Biospecimen collection, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Statements that other substances were absent from 'nearly all' patients apply to the samples tested for each; for petroleum distillates only 12 patients were tested.

reporting_issues.issue: The three patients without vitamin E acetate are described as probable cases; the paper does not state that all 25 confirmed cases were positive, which follows from the counts.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 100% in confirmed cases is an editors' deduction; the percentage given in the paper is 94% for all 51.

reporting_issues.issue: The text read is the author manuscript (available in PMC from 20 February 2021); the printed NEJM version of 20 December 2019 (volume 382, pages 697 to 705) may differ in wording or figures.
reporting_issues.consequence: Locators refer to the manuscript's paragraphs; they should be re-checked against the publisher version if a page number is needed.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7032996 (author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1 to 4, acknowledgments and reference list read as text; the Supplementary Appendix, a PDF, was not opened; the publisher's disclosure forms were not opened)
